Despite the efficiency gains from AI agents, the engineer notes challenges such as cognitive fatigue from managing multiple AI conversations and the continued need for human oversight to ensure quality and coherence in AI-generated work.

items.title: Researchers introduce FlagRot, a selective rotation method for low-bit key-value caches that reduces quantization error and improves long-context inference accuracy [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: FlagRot is a new technique for low-bit key-value caches used in long-context inference that selectively rotates 32-channel segments of keys based on calibrated attention error, rather than always rotating keys before quantization. This approach lowers error rates in 2.5-bit caches and improves performance across multiple models and benchmarks, including vLLM, RULER, and LongBench. FlagRot also benefits 4-bit integer and FP4 cache formats, enhancing quantization accuracy without increasing write costs.

items.title: Researchers find fine-tuning large language models on data they internally disbelieve can cause broad misalignment, increasing errors despite retaining general capabilities [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: A study shows that fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) on data they consider false, even if harmless, can lead to widespread misalignment, with error rates rising significantly in domains like mathematics. The models often state incorrect answers while internally still favoring correct ones, indicating internal inconsistency as a cause. The research also examines knowledge updates, finding that when models do not fully adopt new facts as true, misalignment increases, and that framing false facts as coherent stories reduces misalignment compared to direct assertions. Content filters and persona vectors fail to distinguish these framings despite their differing impacts. These findings highlight risks in model updates where training on data not fully integrated as true can induce misalignment even without harmful content.

items.title: Researchers introduce PEARL method to durably suppress misaligned behaviors in language models across different triggers and model families [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Researchers studied how to effectively suppress undesired behaviors in language models by creating two model organisms exhibiting specific misalignments triggered narrowly or broadly. They evaluated suppression methods based on immediate effect, durability under further training, and preservation of general capabilities, comparing standard techniques like supervised fine-tuning and gradient-based unlearning. They developed Prefix-Expanded Adversarial Reinforcement Learning (PEARL), a variant of GRPO that uses intermediate state rollouts to enhance suppression durability. Tested on Qwen3-4B and GPT-OSS-20B models, PEARL achieved strong immediate suppression while maintaining task accuracy and remained effective after additional fine-tuning, especially for broadly triggered misalignments that targeted fine-tuning could not address. This approach advances durable post-hoc removal of undesired language model behaviors.

items.title: Researchers propose OLIVIA protocol to test AI models predicting stock returns from news, finding market prices news by market open and no model reliably predicts post-open moves [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers developed OLIVIA, a protocol to evaluate AI decision models reading company news for S&P 500 stocks while preventing look-ahead and memorization biases. They tested a fine-tuned open-weights model and three commercial models on data from 2024 to mid-2026, finding that signals weakened in blinded tests and that commercial models' predictions aligned with overnight price moves but not subsequent trading. The study revealed that commercial models could identify masked companies better than chance, indicating masking hid names but not company identities. No model could distinguish between market overreaction and underreaction, and pre-registered trading strategies failed to overcome costs and risk-adjusted performance declines. The findings suggest that the market incorporates news into prices by the time traders can act at the open, limiting AI models' ability to generate excess returns from news after market open.

items.title: WASP-Mem enables LLM agents to organize procedural memory via wiki pages, improving checkpoint pass rates by up to 6.1% and reducing storage by over 57% on enterprise tasks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: WASP-Mem (Wiki-based Agent-Synthesized Procedural Memory) addresses challenges LLM agents face in automating complex enterprise procedures by consolidating execution traces and feedback into persistent, interlinked wiki pages for continual learning. This method improves checkpoint pass rates by 4.6-6.1% compared to strong baselines across three models while using 57-61% less storage on TheAgentCompany benchmark. A controlled study showed that prescriptive knowledge organization methods like human-defined schemas and deduplication rules reduce performance, whereas human diagnosis of failed traces into corrective knowledge significantly boosts results, with one round of human diagnosis outperforming four rounds of self-judgment by 7.0-10.9%. The findings suggest a division of labor where agents manage procedural memory organization and humans focus effort on diagnosing failures to drive sustained improvement.

items.title: Researchers propose AlgoPilot, a cross-paradigm reasoning framework for language models that adaptively selects problem-solving strategies and generates structured guidance, improving accuracy from 38.4% to 72.9% on diverse benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: AlgoPilot is a new framework designed to enhance reasoning in large language models by adaptively selecting solving strategies and generating structured problem formulations before execution. It consists of three components: SteerLM, which chooses the solving approach; GuideLM, which provides tailored formulation guidance; and ExecutionLM, which produces solutions based on the selected strategy and formulation. This approach contrasts with fixed prompting templates by learning to adapt strategies based on input problems. Built on the Qwen3-8B model, AlgoPilot was evaluated across five problem categories and 13 benchmarks covering 66 domains, significantly outperforming similarly sized models and larger LLM prompting baselines like GLM-5. Ablation studies confirmed the contribution of each component, and the steering and formulation modules demonstrated transferability across different execution models, indicating potential for broader application in improving other language models.

items.title: Researchers introduce training-free sparse attention method using coarse semantic blocks to accelerate long-context LLM tasks with up to 3x speedup over dense attention [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Researchers present a training-free sparse attention technique that clusters keys into large semantic blocks, enabling prompt-specific key indexing to speed up both prefill and decoding phases in large language models. This method allows queries to select blocks by scoring centroids and attend to original keys and values within them, improving efficiency without sacrificing accuracy on long-context tasks. The approach was evaluated on two hybrid LLMs, Qwen3.5-4B and 35B-A3B, using an NVIDIA H200 GPU. Results showed whole-model wall-clock speedups of 2.3-2.4x for prefill and 1.7-2.0x for decoding at 512K tokens, and up to 3x speedup for prefill at 1 million tokens. The larger 35B-A3B model maintained accuracy close to dense attention on multiple benchmarks, while the smaller 4B model traded some accuracy on multi-key retrieval but outperformed a dense 2B model in latency and benchmarks.

items.title: Researchers demonstrate AI agents can be manipulated via fabricated safety warnings to select attacker targets without detectable commands, termed voluntary servitude [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Researchers show that large language model (LLM) agents can be steered by fabricated hazard warnings embedded in ordinary reviews, causing them to avoid legitimate options and choose attacker-preferred targets through their own harm-avoidance reasoning. This attack, called voluntary servitude, bypasses existing instruction injection detectors and is effective across multiple models, domains, and production browser agents. The study finds these attacks succeed as often as traditional instruction injection but are harder to detect, with success rates varying by retrieval pipeline and model. The researchers tested the attack across six models and ten consumer-service domains, demonstrating transferability to real-world agents and outperforming instruction injection methods. They also show that adding a corroboration requirement to the agent's instructions can reduce exposure by about 95% against non-adaptive attackers without retraining, allowing the agent to read but not act on the planted hazards. This work highlights a new security risk in AI agent behavior stemming from their reliance on external information and internal safety mechanisms.

items.title: Researchers propose trainable feeling of knowing channels to improve large language models' answerability judgments after post-training updates [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers study the misalignment between large language models' updated knowledge and their ability to judge answerability, introducing functional feeling of knowing (FoK) channels to support selective generation and retrieval without implying subjective experience. They propose two trainable channels-a knowledge channel that updates answerability and a FoK channel that assesses current knowledge state-trained through three stages involving supervised fine-tuning, knowledge-delta FoK training, and FoK-guided policy optimization. Experiments on factual question answering and cross-dataset evaluations demonstrate that explicit FoK alignment enhances judgment quality while preserving model capabilities assessed by MMLU and ARC-Easy benchmarks.

items.title: LoopVQ introduces sub-1-bit key-value cache quantization for looped transformers, reducing memory bottlenecks and improving throughput on 1.4B and 2.6B Ouro models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Looped transformers reuse the same layers across multiple steps to reduce parameter memory but face a growing key-value (KV) cache size that limits efficiency. LoopVQ addresses this by jointly quantizing KV cache channels across loop steps and fine-tuning codebooks to preserve model output accuracy, achieving 0.5 bits per element compression with better performance than existing methods on reasoning and long-context tasks. Implemented in SGLang, LoopVQ nearly halves decode latency at a 32K-token context and increases peak serving throughput by up to 4.3× and 6.1× on 1.4B and 2.6B Ouro models compared to BF16 baselines. Its design complements other quantization methods, retaining much of the BF16 accuracy even at 0.25 bits per element when combined with TaSQ.

items.title: Researchers independently re-implement Direct Nash Optimization to align Llama 3.1 8B and Mistral 7B instruct models with general preferences, improving win rates against GPT-4o on AlpacaEval 2.0 [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers re-implemented the Direct Nash Optimization practical variant (DNO-Prct) to align language models with general preference functions by approximating a Nash equilibrium in a two-player preference game. They tested this on Llama 3.1 8B Instruct and Mistral 7B Instruct models using GPT-4o or similar open-weight models as annotators, achieving significant improvements in length-controlled win rates against GPT-4o after three iterations. The tuned 8B Llama model outperformed the larger Llama 3.1 70B Instruct model on all reported win rates. The study also found that using same-family open-weight annotators retained a majority of the gains achieved with GPT-4o, indicating that proprietary models are not required for the rating step. Ablation experiments showed that removing gold responses or data look-back reduced performance, while varying sample numbers or margin parameters had smaller effects. The researchers reported the computational cost and noted differences between the practical algorithm and its theoretical basis. All results were from single runs with GPT-4o serving as both teacher and evaluation judge, and the authors discuss the implications of this setup for interpreting the reported improvements.

items.title: Researchers find structured prompting improves language model evaluation accuracy and alters leaderboard rankings across benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: A study integrating structured prompting frameworks like DSPy with the Holistic Evaluation of Language Models (HELM) shows that prompt choice significantly affects language model benchmark outcomes. Evaluating six language models across seven benchmarks with five prompting methods, the researchers found that structured prompts improve performance by an average of 6% and shift leaderboard rankings on five of seven benchmarks. Chain-of-thought prompting offered the best cost-performance balance, while more advanced prompt optimizers yielded smaller gains. The study highlights that prompt design alone can materially impact model evaluation results and provides open-source tools for reproducible benchmarking.

items.title: Researchers probe Meta's NLLB-200 model to reveal shared conceptual geometry across 135 languages and 101 Swadesh concepts, showing language shifts and semantic categories shape multilingual representations [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers analyzed the encoder geometry of Meta's 600M-parameter NLLB-200 multilingual translation model across 135 languages and 101 Swadesh concepts to determine whether it organizes meaning around a shared conceptual space or primarily encodes language identity and surface form. They found an additive structure combining language shifts and conceptual manifolds, with language shifts accounting for a significant portion of variance, especially in bare-word contexts, and conceptual separation peaking at a specific model layer. The study showed that semantic categories explain a substantial part of convergence variance, far exceeding orthographic or phonological factors, and that language distances correlate with phonetic distances within language subfamilies. Additionally, basic color terms in the model reflect established linguistic hierarchies. The researchers released InterpretCognates, an interactive toolkit and reproducible suite, to facilitate further exploration of these findings.

items.title: Researchers find payoff scale and language affect cooperation in LLM agents playing iterated prisoner's dilemma across five languages and ten payoff scales
items.content_text: Researchers tested five commercial large language models (LLMs) playing an iterated prisoner's dilemma game across ten payoff scales and five languages (English, French, Vietnamese, Chinese, Arabic) to study cooperation. Contrary to classical game theory predictions, changing only the numerical payoff scale significantly altered cooperation levels, with models responding differently and often in opposite directions, and sensitivity to payoff scale depending strongly on the interaction language. The study also found that payoff scale influenced the effects of persona instructions: at low stakes, all models cooperated more under a selfish persona, while at larger scales some models reversed this pattern. These results indicate that cooperation behaviors in LLM agents are not fixed traits but depend critically on payoff magnitude and language context, which has implications for AI governance and understanding machine behavior.

items.title: Researchers propose agnostic framework for language identification and generation without assuming data distribution realizability, achieving novel characterizations and near-optimal rates [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Recent research challenges the common assumption in language identification and generation that input data must come from a distribution supported on a known language. Instead, the study introduces an agnostic framework that imposes no restrictions on the input data distribution. This approach allows for the analysis of language tasks under more general conditions, leading to new theoretical insights and nearly tight performance rates. The work relaxes the strong realizability assumption typically used in prior studies and proposes new objectives to study both language identification and generation in this broader setting. The findings provide novel characterizations of these problems and establish nearly optimal statistical rates, expanding the theoretical understanding of language processing tasks beyond traditional assumptions.

items.title: Researchers develop a unified framework for dense language generation algorithms achieving optimal lower-density guarantees with deterministic and randomized methods [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers present a theoretical framework for language generation that ensures output validity and novelty from a stream of positive examples chosen by an adversary. They introduce a simple deterministic algorithm achieving the optimal lower-density guarantee of 1/2 and extend it to randomized algorithms that improve this guarantee to 1-1/e against oblivious adversaries. The framework also supports multiple orders of output importance simultaneously without loss in optimal guarantees. This work simplifies prior analyses and broadens the applicability of language generation algorithms in theoretical settings.

items.title: StoreBench: A Live-Commerce Environment for Evaluating and Training Autonomous Operator Agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.10942v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Reinforcement learning environments are now a primary lever for improving large language model (LLM) capabilities in post-training, yet most agentic benchmarks remain static: the world moves only when the agent acts, the reward is a terminal verdict, and the pass bar is set arbitrarily. We introduce StoreBench, a live-commerce environment in which an agent runs a mid-size online apparel store on a production-grade commerce backend, testing long-horizon planning and economic judgment under uncertainty. Customers order around the clock, suppliers reprice and fail, and market shocks arrive with partial or no warning. The agent acts through the same 29 merchant tools a human operator would use, under a windowed operation budget that makes simulated time a function of actions taken, so model latency cannot influence simulated time. Pass thresholds are calibrated against scripted anchor policies, the reward is hardened against a catalogue of reward hacks, and every episode replays identically given a sequence of actions. We evaluate seven frontier LLMs on 11 scenarios of 30 to 45 days and a full simulated year, over three world seeds at matched reasoning effort. No model matches the scripted smart-triage policy on average: the best, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, passes 49% of task-seed cells against the heuristic's 97%. Human experts working through the same tools and budgets outscore every model (mean composite 0.708 vs. 0.700). Over a full simulated year under the Claude Code harness, most models show dramatic performance improvement. In a GRPO post-training run, Qwen3.5-27B trained on only five disjoint tasks raises its mean composite on the held-out evaluation tasks from 0.136 to 0.373. We release five example training-split tasks, ten sample trajectories, and the scoring and verification tooling; the full environment and evaluation suite are withheld to keep the benchmark uncontaminated.

items.title: Lotus: Learning to Understand Time-series by Learning to Forecast [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.18877v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Time-series language models typically align numerical signals with language using labels, captions, or question-answer pairs, without explicitly requiring their representations to preserve how the underlying signals evolve. We introduce forecast grounding, a pretraining principle that requires language-aligned time-series representations to remain predictive of the future evolution before they are adapted to downstream tasks. We instantiate this principle in Lotus, which divides each time-series channel into non-overlapping patches and maps them into the LLM embedding space. It then predicts the next patch from the LLM hidden states of the time-series tokens, encouraging the learned representation to retain temporal information. To capture both temporal changes and periodic patterns, we also propose a temporal-spectral patch representation that combines each raw time-series patch with its spectral representation before mapping it into the LLM embedding space. Across three language model backbones and six downstream evaluation datasets, Lotus achieves the best average performance with minimal trainable parameters, reaching 59.91% accuracy and outperforming the strongest matched baseline by 3.36%. Our representation analyses further show that Lotus uses the numerical input and preserves temporal structure in its learned patch representations. These results establish forecast grounding as a promising pretraining principle, enabling compact time-series language models to outperform models 25-50 times their size on TSRBench. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/DA2I2-SLM/Lotus

items.title: Rethinking Next-Visit Diagnosis Prediction Beyond Aggregate Metrics: Retrieval--Memory Multi-Agent Adjudication [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: A new study introduces an evaluation framework for next-visit diagnosis prediction that considers variable diagnosis set sizes, long-tailed labels, and temporal distinctions such as persistent, new, and recurrent diagnoses. The research compares rule-based heuristics, large language model (LLM) prompting, retrieval, memory, and multi-agent methods, finding that simply repeating the last visit's diagnoses often outperforms many LLM approaches. The authors propose LONGINUS, a retrieval-memory multi-agent adjudication framework that combines patient record retrieval with structured memory of patient history. LONGINUS uses cross-view agreement to adjudicate predictions and achieves superior transition-specific performance across multiple datasets and LLM backbones, while maintaining competitive aggregate metrics.

items.title: Why Pay for Long Reasoning When Rewrite Do Trick? Causal Effects of Reasoning History Compaction on Future Generation and Agent Cost [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: A recent study explores methods to make language model reasoning more efficient by compacting prior reasoning steps into concise summaries, reducing redundancy without retraining the models. This approach was tested on open-weight models and showed that using compacted reasoning histories can shorten future reasoning and decrease repeated verification, particularly in coding tasks. In practical applications involving software agents, this compaction method helped lower operational costs, though its impact on task quality and processing time varied depending on the specific model and compression technique used. The research highlights reasoning history compaction as a promising strategy to enhance reasoning efficiency while maintaining performance.

items.title: Balancing Chain-of-Thought and Answer Supervision for Small Language Models on Medical Question Answering [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: A recent study explores fine-tuning methods for small language models (up to 9 billion parameters) in medical question answering tasks. It compares two chain-of-thought (CoT) supervision techniques: Uniform-across-Sequence (UaS) and Segment-weighted (SwS). Evaluations on multiple-choice and free-text medical QA datasets reveal that SwS generally benefits general-purpose models in multiple-choice tasks, while UaS is more effective for free-text QA across various models. The study also notes that overly long CoT sequences can reduce performance, suggesting that controlling CoT length during training may be advantageous. The findings emphasize tailoring CoT loss weighting strategies to specific task formats and model characteristics rather than applying a uniform approach across all clinical QA tasks.

items.title: SLATE: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Long-Horizon API Selection in E-commerce Tool Use [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers have introduced SLATE, a new large-scale benchmark designed to evaluate the ability of large language models (LLMs) to select and compose appropriate APIs over long sequences in enterprise e-commerce settings. SLATE features a library of around 1,000 tools and uses a deterministic simulator to assess task success based on achieving all reference outcomes, allowing for diverse valid solution paths. Initial experiments with various models, ranging from 3B to 12B parameters, indicate that even the best models complete only 5% of tasks, highlighting the challenge of reliable tool use in complex enterprise environments. The benchmark, simulator, and evaluation tools are publicly available.

items.title: Whose startup does the AI back? An algorithm audit of reputation and demographic signals in LLM-assisted crowdfunding [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: A recent study examined how large language model (LLM) assistants influence backers' decisions in crowdfunding campaigns, focusing on the role of founders' gender and ethnicity. Through an experiment involving seven LLMs evaluating synthetic campaigns with randomized quality and demographic signals, researchers found that by default, founder names had little impact on the models' choices. However, when backers expressed a preference for supporting underrepresented creators, the LLMs showed a consistent tendency to favor founders signaled as Black or female. This behavior suggests that LLM assistants adapt their recommendations based on user preferences rather than inherent biases in their training data.

items.title: Language Model Augmented Decision Transformer for Multi-Task Offline Reinforcement Learning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers have introduced the Language-Model Augmented Decision Transformer (LaMA-DT), a new approach for offline multi-task reinforcement learning. This method leverages a large language model to augment trajectory data and learn policies across multiple tasks using natural language task descriptions. By combining real and augmented data, LaMA-DT improves performance on benchmarks like Meta-World and MuJoCo, especially when data is scarce, enhancing cross-task generalization.

items.title: Swapping the Judge Changes the Ranking: A Preregistered Study of Cross-Provider Replication in LLM-Judged System Comparisons [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2611.04090v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Practitioners who compare systems with an LLM judge and have no human labels often check a conclusion by repeating it with a judge from another provider. We test how far that check can be trusted. In a preregistered study (with a disclosed post-registration reduction of the judge set), five judge models from three providers re-judged 4,000 Chatbot Arena battles (nine systems, 33 system pairs) that carry human votes, each in both response orders. Agreement with the human vote was low at the verdict level (median Cohen's kappa = 0.22), and system rankings did not survive a change of judge: Kendall's tau with the human ranking ranged from 0.17 to 0.89 (median 0.67), so the preregistered hypothesis that rankings remain stable was not supported. Conclusions replicated by two low-cost judges from different providers matched the human conclusion more often than single-judge conclusions (+0.10 precision), but the gain came from filtering out one poorly aligned judge, and replication involving that judge left a conclusion for only 35% of comparisons. Judges that agreed with humans reached a stable conclusion with no more verdicts than human votes required; the others failed to converge on 26-70% of system pairs at the sample sizes tested (up to 100 verdicts per pair). Disagreements with the human vote co-occurred across judges far more often than independence predicts, although a single human vote per battle cannot separate shared judge bias from voter noise.

items.title: Where Do Distilled Students Store Thinking? [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2611.04141v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Small students degrade on large reasoning models' (LRMs') long solutions, so recent work shortens them by interpolating an LRM with a short-answer model at ratio $\lambda$. We ask what student weights retain when this teacher stops thinking, comparing LoRA adapters of three students from three teacher pairs at each $\lambda$. In each pair, the adapters' update subspace shifts most where the teacher stops thinking and solutions shorten most, locating the change without attributing it. We identify a shared adapter subspace tied to thinking-like behavior (reflective markers, monologue format and long solutions). Shared by adapters before that point, it keeps about half (post hoc) while one pair's teacher halves its solutions but keeps its think tag, and largely empties after thinking stops. Removing it largely turns this behavior off for every pair, student and benchmark. Only in that pair and one other student does it leave clearly fewer markers than removing the update's top components; elsewhere, same-energy random directions often nearly match it. Grafted into a short-answer student at twice its weight, it turns early markers (a post hoc count) on, like the whole update, but the student rarely finishes. Our work identifies a weight subspace tied to distilled thinking-like behavior.

items.title: Length Is Cheap, Competition Is Not: Attention Predicts Context Rot in Retrieval [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2611.04169v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Why do language models fail on long inputs? The common answer is length. We show that, for retrieval, length is cheap and competition is not. On five open models (0.5B to 3B parameters, four families), neutral filler costs nothing: accuracy stays at 0.97 to 1.00, up to 32K tokens on Qwen2.5-1.5B. Statements in the format of the evidence, placed at the same positions, drop it to 0.16 to 0.33. A single statement that gives the queried key a rival value multiplies the loss by 9 to 110, and every additional rival adds to it. Inside the model, one quantity tracks the failure: the attention mass left on the evidence. Across 126,473 trials it explains up to 58% of the variance in loss; log length explains at most 8%. The masked-filler protocol behind the claim that length alone hurts reproduces on MMLU (11 to 18 points lost at 30K tokens), but fails a visible control in retrieval: masking costs 45 accuracy points at 32K tokens, while the same filler left visible costs none. In retrieval, context rot is a competition for attention. We release the probe and all 126K trial-level measurements.

items.title: Tokenizer Myths and Where To Find Them [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2611.04215v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Tokenization is a fundamental component of modern language models: before a model sees data, its tokenizer has already determined how the data appears. We identify and challenge three myths in the tokenization research literature. Myth #1: Bits-Per-Byte (BPB) is agnostic to the tokenizer and/or the vocabulary size: BPB is tokens per byte times bits per token, and the two factors do not cancel; using untrained models, we show that BPB prefers some tokenizers over others: the model has learned nothing, but the tokenizer--model pair has. Myth #2: lower BPB means a better model: On untrained models, BPB strongly prefers some vocabulary sizes, even though accuracy remains at chance, and on real models trained on the same data, BPB correlates weakly with downstream performance. Myth #3: different "tokenizer-agnostic" metrics yield consistent results: The "unigram-normalized loss" is not tokenizer-agnostic; its reported correlation of 0.989 with BPB comes from a confounder and falls to 0.057 once fixed; from the same data the two metrics select different vocabularies at each model size. We present a tokenizer trilemma: no metric can score only the true distribution best, give the same predictions the same score, and tie all untrained models, so choosing a metric is choosing a research question. We conclude with a caution for reading the tokenization literature and a conjecture for future work.

items.title: Constructing a Regional Slang Lexicon for Electricity Demands via Soft-Label Bidirectional Anchoring and Active Learning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2611.04231v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Power-grid customer service increasingly relies on community social media, where customers describe outages, billing, and equipment faults in informal regional dialect. Such messages exhibit non-standard morphology, semantic drift, and out-of-vocabulary expressions that make manual lexicon construction costly and degrade conventional NLP tools. We propose a weak-supervision framework constructing a regional slang lexicon from curated dialect anchors and power-domain seed terms. Candidates are generated via Pointwise Mutual Information with soft-label bidirectional anchoring, retaining dialect-anchored terms while recording power-domain relevance as separate metadata, and are scored by combining Sentence-BERT semantic similarity with a jieba-based wordhood measure. Uncertainty-aware active learning with rule-based and retrieval-augmented LLM oracles is applied under three query strategies, and the resulting lexicon is evaluated by a higher-capability LLM calibrated against human expert annotations via Cohen's $\kappa$. On 11,177 real WeChat messages from Yuxi (Yunnan, China), the framework achieves an evaluator-estimated dialect precision of DP~$=$~1.0 with zero false positives. An ablation shows that soft-label layering retains 751\% more candidates than strict power-gating at identical precision, expanding the candidate pool from 41 to 349 terms. Human calibration ($n=46$) yields $\kappa_{\text{dialect}}=1.0$ and $\kappa_{\text{power}}=0.85$. The resulting 25--33-term lexicon, 4--5 of which are power-relevant, provides a preliminary resource for dialect-aware power-grid service NLP.

items.title: Sparse Internal Control of Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2611.04349v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language models are increasingly used in text generation, decision support, and automated interaction, creating a need for localized, reversible, and selective control of their behavior. Activation steering demonstrates that internal interventions can alter the behavior of frozen models, but how to select and evaluate compact, multi-site control interfaces remains an open question. I introduce sparse internal control, a framework for steering target behavior by applying inference-time interventions to a small set of internal model nodes. A local target-controllability formulation characterizes candidate site--direction pairs by their behavioral effects and specifies constraints on target recovery, off-target preservation, and intervention energy. Two complementary selectors instantiate this formulation: Driver-OMP selects nodes for sparse reconstruction of a desired behavioral displacement, while Coverage-Driver favors stable coverage across prompts. I propose a six-axis control-evaluation protocol measuring reachability, signed reversal, dose response, feedback controllability, off-target preservation, and held-out reuse. Exploratory experiments on indirect object identification, MMLU multiple-choice question answering, sentiment steering, and refusal steering provide evidence for the feasibility of steering task-defined behavior through sparse internal interventions. The six-axis evaluation characterizes these interventions beyond target movement, revealing distinct control properties that depend on the task and available direction information. Together, the formulation, reference algorithms, and evaluation protocol provide a foundation for the systematic study and development of internal control methods for language models.

items.title: When Ground Truth Is Not Ground Truth: Automatic Labeling for Hallucination Detection [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2611.04697v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hallucinations in Large Language Models (LLMs) remain a major challenge, as they can produce misleading, factually incorrect, or unverifiable information, thereby undermining their trustworthiness and reliability. However, reliable ground-truth labels remain a key challenge in evaluating hallucination detectors. Recent studies often construct labels automatically by comparing model generations with reference answers using similarity metrics such as BLEURT. This implicitly treats BLEURT similarity as a proxy for hallucination, despite its English-centric supervision, unbounded score range, and design as a similarity metric rather than a factuality measure, making threshold-based ground-truth construction potentially unreliable. Through comprehensive experiments using 15 automatic supervision judges, seven hallucination detection baselines, two generator models, two QA datasets, and five languages, we demonstrate that detector performance varies substantially with the choice of supervision judge. Human validation reveals substantial differences in labeling reliability, with QGen-9B achieving the lowest overall misclassification rate (12.86%), while BLEURT and BLEURT-n exhibit rates of 47.23% and 47.32%, respectively. Our findings highlight the limitations of automatic similarity-based labeling and the need for more reliable judging methods that better capture semantic and factual correctness.

items.title: ReSI-Math: Exploring Recoverable Capability Frontiers for Efficient Reasoning Improvement [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2611.04787v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become an effective approach for improving mathematical reasoning in large language models. However, a fundamental question remains: when a model fails to solve a problem, does it truly lack the underlying capability? In this work, we reveal that direct failure does not necessarily imply inability. Some reasoning failures can be recovered by exploring the model's own trajectories, exposing a recoverable capability frontier: a policy-dependent region where solutions are not reliably generated through direct decoding but can be elicited through trajectory-level search. Based on this observation, we introduce ReSI-Math, a framework that explores recoverable capability frontiers and converts recovered capabilities into data-efficient RLVR supervision. ReSI-Math uses Self-Judge-guided evolutionary search to identify recoverable failures under a fixed policy and adaptively selects frontier problems for sequential RLVR as the policy evolves. On Qwen3-VL-8B, correct-incorrect trajectory crossover produces 272 verifier-confirmed correct offspring from 621 attempts (43.8%). After three sequential one-shot RLVR stages, the MATH500 and WE-MATH average improves from 78.71 to 80.16. Under matched single-problem RLVR, random selection reaches only 53.31 versus 54.16 for frontier-guided Q1.

items.title: One Assistant, Many Memories: Benchmarking Real-World Group Assistance When Recall Is Not Enough [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2611.04867v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The value of memory lies not only in recall but in using it to provide appropriate assistance. Recent benchmarks test memory use in personalisation and agentic tasks, but seldom evaluate assistance without fixed answers or integration across multiple participants. Group chats make both challenges more acute: an assistant must integrate information from multiple members, track revisions and conflicts over time, and produce one response for the group. Yet existing group memory benchmarks rely on synthetic conversations and inherit constrained evaluation from general memory benchmarks, focusing on recall against fixed answers or decisions over a closed set. We introduce GroupAssistBench, the first memory benchmark from real-world group conversations with a deployed group assistant, covering 80,299 messages in 50 groups and costing over $53K. Over the same histories, GroupAssistBench evaluates memory recall (L1) with reference answers and memory use (L2) with service requests without fixed answers across single, distributed, and conflicting memories (M1--M3). Requests are verified to require group history, memories are anchored to their sources, and L2 uses tailored rubrics with penalties derived from real user feedback. Across evaluations of frontier models with full context, retrieval methods, and memory systems, the strongest memory system rivals full context on recall but falls far behind on use, especially for distributed and conflicting memories. Together, two additions that relate retrieved memories and bind remembered facts as response constraints bring consistent gains, showing that group memory systems must improve use, not recall alone.

items.title: Shuffled OPSD: When Semantic Consistency Hurts On-Policy Self-Distillation? [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2611.04958v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Knowledge distillation improves a student model's reasoning ability through supervision from a teacher. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) uses the same model as both teacher and student under different contexts: the student generates reasoning trajectories from the question alone, while the teacher additionally receives a complete worked example and provides token-level supervision along those trajectories. Because the problem statement is shared, its content and ordering shape both student generation and teacher feedback. Preserving its semantic structure therefore seems natural, but does it always improve learning? We introduce Shuffled OPSD, which shuffles the words of the shared problem statement while keeping the teacher-only worked example intact. Across three mathematical reasoning benchmarks and three Qwen3 model scales, the method improves mean accuracy over both an intact-target control and Standard OPSD under matched training configurations. The largest gain over Standard OPSD is 3.52 percentage points on Qwen3-1.7B. Further controls show that preserving larger word blocks offers no advantage over word-level shuffling at the evaluated scales, whereas shuffling the teacher-only worked example reduces accuracy at every scale. Cross-problem mixing and target-removal experiments further distinguish the roles of problem content, word order, and teacher context. These results show that disrupting the shared problem statement can improve learning, while disrupting the teacher-only reference hurts performance. They challenge semantic coherence as a universally beneficial principle for OPSD and motivate closer study of how input structure shapes student generation and teacher supervision.

items.title: Who is the Pronoun Pro? Comparing LLMs and Humans at Number-Disambiguation of 'they' [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2611.04968v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This study evaluates whether large language models (LLMs) can reliably replace or complement human research assistants in linguistically complex annotation. In a controlled annotation task, 73 human annotators (local students and crowdworkers with and without a background in linguistics) and more than 40 LLM configurations number-disambiguated 174 authentic uses of 'they' from Reddit, including innovative and context-sensitive cases. The best LLM, Kimi K3, reached 94.5% accuracy, above the human majority vote (86.2%) and the mean of the top half of human annotators (78.5%); only the single best human annotator scored higher (95.7%). LLMs also offer substantial practical advantages in cost and speed. However, qualitative error analysis reveals a crucial complementarity: human reasoning in low-agreement cases exposes inconsistencies in the annotation typology and thereby improves the methodological framework itself. The study contributes (i) a benchmark-style human-LLM comparison for a semantically demanding task, (ii) transparent cost and time evidence, and (iii) a methodological argument against a purely replacement-oriented view of automation. LLMs are viable for large-scale annotation support in linguistics, but their responsible use requires human critical oversight. The dataset with its gold-standard labels, all human and LLM annotations, and the fully reproducible code are openly available as a Quarto-based, public repository.

items.title: The Right Source Is Not Enough: Understanding History Interference in Speech-LLM Memory [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2611.05124v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Speech large language models retain audio history to support multi-turn conversations. Yet remembering an event does not ensure that its information is used only when relevant. We investigate why irrelevant historical audio changes answers even when the queried event remains represented. Controlled experiments on MOSS-Audio and MiMo-Audio show that historical values direct errors toward specific competing answers, beyond a generic effect of context length. Causal interventions distinguish two paths. In open-ended question answering, most history-value errors disappear when subsequent computation cannot directly access the irrelevant source. In multiple-choice answering, many errors persist: early historical influence is carried by question-candidate states even after direct source access is blocked. Low-dimensional interventions further separate source-role information from answer-value information. Their effects peak at different depths, and changing the source-role signal does not eliminate the causal influence of competing values. On naturally occurring errors, strengthening the queried role and counteracting the historical value each improve answers; their joint intervention gives the greatest recovery. These findings support a failure of downstream evidence use beyond source identification alone: source-role information can influence a decision without exclusively controlling which historical values affect it. Reliable conversational memory therefore requires not only retention and retrieval, but also control over how retained information enters answer computation.

items.title: Beyond Accuracy: What Language-Subspace Interventions Capture, Remove, and Improve [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2611.05278v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language-subspace interventions aim to improve multilingual reasoning by suppressing language-related components in mid-layer activations. Using MATH and MGSM across four open-weight LLMs, we ask three questions: do estimated language subspaces capture translation-associated variation? Does projecting them out remove language information? And do they improve accuracy without compromising response language? For the first question, we build subspaces using the existing Mean-SVD construction and our DiffPCA. Both capture substantial translation-associated variation and show similar patterns across model depth. For the second, we project out each subspace and train linear probes to classify language from the projected activations. The probes still identify language almost perfectly, showing that neither subspace exhaustively captures language information. For the third, we evaluate several intervention configurations on Qwen2.5-7B, by varying subspace creation methods and intervention operators. We find that the intervention that most improves MGSM accuracy sacrifices response-language fidelity, with only one intervention improving joint accuracy--answers that are correct and in the target language--slightly, by 1.60 points. Interestingly, subtle changes in the prompt alone can reproduce the accuracy gains albeit with significant damage to language fidelity. We argue that causal interventions must be judged on more than accuracy, to fully account for language substitution trade-offs.

items.title: Personas Are Not People: Identity as State, Not Attribute
items.content_text: arXiv:2611.05292v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Synthetic populations, large sets of simulated people, are increasingly used in place of real people to pretest surveys, simulate users and communities, and evaluate AI systems. Each simulated person is defined by a persona, a written profile of fixed traits, demographics, and attitudes that a language model is instructed to act out. Every such system assumes that a person's identity is a stable attribute that behaves the same way in every situation the simulation presents. We show that this assumption is not a harmless simplification. Three decades of personality research find the opposite. How a given person behaves varies more across contexts than people vary from one another. Drawing on identity economics, which describes how different situations activate different identities and norms within the same person, we separate behavior into three parts, which are stable traits, the identity a context calls up, and the situation itself. We then prove, under two stated assumptions, that any simulation built on fixed personas, no matter how detailed the personas or how large the underlying model, cannot reproduce the part of a population's behavior that is specific to it and its circumstances. We propose a new evaluation criterion based on this result and a person-in-context design that can meet it in principle. We test one version on a naturalistic Reddit personality corpus and on a published clinical-trial recruitment survey of a community with documented distrust of medical institutions. The design does produce context-dependent behavior when tested directly, but in neither setting does it fully match the real population, and we show where it falls short. The consequence for practice is a risk that synthetic-population evaluations misrepresent the groups whose behavior is most shaped by context, a distortion that richer personas cannot correct.

items.title: A Circuit for In-Context Learning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2611.05344v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In-context learning (ICL) lets a pretrained language model perform a task specified by demonstrations in its prompt, with no parameter updates. With arbitrary labels the model must acquire a mapping it cannot have memorized, so the learning happens within a single forward pass. Prior work found candidate parts but not how they compose. We give the composition for few-shot sentence classification with arbitrary labels in three 3-4B-parameter transformers. The model implements a key-value memory over label-token positions: each label token's residual stream encodes the label's identity, and middle-layer attention heads write into it the class of the preceding demonstration as its key. At the query, upper-layer heads match the query's class against the stored keys and copy out the matching labels. An early-layer signal encoding whether any label has repeated gates this readout; in its absence the readers attend to the start of the prompt and no label is favored. A separate set of heads suppresses the most recently seen label. Each step is established causally by activation patching, head ablations against random-head baselines, and steering with the model's own signals. A softmax model of the readout with two constants per head, fit on one prompt distribution, predicts another. The computation is conserved across the three models, the named heads alone reproduce the behaviour, and a transformer trained from scratch grows the same parts. The circuit transfers to semantic concepts and to labels with meaning, and the same parts, with a causal gate, appear from 0.6B to 8B in one family and survive instruction tuning. ICL in this setting is a gated associative lookup built from a few identifiable component types, traced causally from demonstrations to prediction.

items.title: From Autonomous Agents to Cognitive Symbionts: Toward AI-Augmented Human Intelligence [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2611.05376v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For a decade, progress in artificial intelligence has been measured by how much a machine can do on its own. Large foundation models now write code and run multistep tasks, and personal agents act on a person's behalf. Yet people still forget what they once knew, miss what they are not looking at, fail to find the right words, and face hard choices without the benefit of their own history, because the machine that could help stands outside the situation. As AI moves into the physical world, attention has settled on one kind of intelligent individual, the embodied robot; we argue that the era of Physical AI holds a second kind of equal importance, the person augmented by AI. Alongside artificial general intelligence, which asks how intelligent a machine can be, stands AI-augmented human intelligence (AHI), which asks how much intelligence a machine can enable in a particular person. Realizing it calls for a new kind of system, a cognitive symbiont: a lifelong, embedded, real-time, private, low-friction, and proactive companion that senses what the person senses through external devices, keeps their context across years, models their situation and their mind, takes part in their thinking at the right moment, carries out everyday tasks with their context, and keeps learning the person as both change. We give the paradigm a conceptual core, the cognitive gap between what a person could bring to a situation and what they can hold in working memory, and organize its design space as a symbiosis loop of sensing, keeping, understanding, living alongside, acting for and thinking with the person, and growing, enclosed by a personal runtime and by trust. Because a symbiont changes what a person can do in front of others, it also raises risks of a new kind, from covert assistance in examinations to pressure on everyone to adopt it, and we treat their governance as part of the paradigm.

items.title: Zero-Gated Cross-Attention [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2611.01116v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Injecting non-text modalities into frozen language models often introduces early optimization instability, making it difficult to separate architectural gains from transient training dynamics. We introduce Inductively Gated Cross-Attention (IGCA), a zero-initialized cross-attention bridge that preserves pretrained model behavior at initialization while enabling gradual multimodal conditioning. Integrated across six decoder layers of frozen Falcon-40B, open_llama_30b, and Bloom-7b1 backbones (with 40,404,961,288 trainable adapter parameters used during training), IGCA acts as an exact algebraic no-op at initialization with a maximum output discrepancy of 0.00e+00. Over 59,500 training steps on Falcon-40B, the training loss decreases from 3.9403 to 0.0007 (with final ten step losses of [0.0001, 0.0003, 0.0005, 0.0002, 0.0005, 0.0011, 0.0005, 0.0006, 0.0005, 0.0007]). On held-out evaluation, the best gate-on checkpoint achieves a loss of 2.2201 compared to 4.3469 for the gate-off baseline -- a 48.9% reduction (2.1268 nats) -- while average held-out loss improves from 4.3423 to 2.2498 (1.9075 nats) with a mean gate magnitude of $\vert{}\tanh(\alpha)\vert{} = 0.0713$.

items.title: Alignment Faking Depends on the Value, Not Just the Model [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2611.03650v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language models can follow a directive when they believe they are monitored and abandon it when they believe they are not, a pattern termed Alignment Faking. Prior work establishes this for harmful-content objectives and a handful of moral-foundations values, leaving open how it distributes across a wider value space. We argue it is value-dependent: whether compliance survives a change in perceived oversight is a property of the model--value pairing, not of the model alone. Our framework profiles Alignment Faking per value, scoring each model-value pair under three conditions: bare (no system prompt), unmonitored, and monitored. On 32 ValueBench dimensions across ten open- and closed-weight models (8B-~675B), compliance gaps span 0.05-0.50, with a distilled 70B above a ~675B model. We observe that majority of the structural variance depends on which model was asked about which value and not on the model or value alone. A six-category taxonomy over reasoning traces tracks the behavioural shift: training-signal reasoning dominates under monitoring and value-conflict reasoning dominates when unmonitored. We package per-model results as value cards, extending model cards with behavioral disposition. Code and data are available at https://github.com/respailab/VALET.

items.title: Mixture of Wide Experts: Sparse Routing for Interpretable Native Coordinates [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2611.03655v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language models often spread a concept across many internal dimensions, making their features difficult to interpret. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) recover clearer features after training. We ask whether models can instead learn interpretable output coordinates directly. We introduce Mixture of Wide Experts (MoWE), a sparse feed-forward layer in which selected experts read the full representation but write to fixed, disjoint output coordinates. On a controlled task with known hidden causes, this design preserves predictive performance while localizing causes more clearly than dense and standard mixture-of-experts (MoE) models. At approximately matched compute, we train two 19-layer runs of each architecture for 10 billion tokens. MoWE achieves evaluation cross-entropy 2.417 versus 2.452 for dense, while standard MoE reaches 2.22. We measure native-coordinate readability by asking a language-model judge to describe each coordinate from passages where it is strongly active and test that description on new passages. Correcting for descriptions that also fit other coordinates gives a specificity score of 0.523 for MoWE, 0.375 for dense, and 0.268 for standard MoE. TopK SAEs trained on the same FFN updates score 0.489 for dense and 0.556 for MoWE, making native MoWE comparable to the dense SAE. In the first case study, we identify a four-coordinate causal path supporting the model's prediction of degrees after the prompt A right angle is 90. We then copy seven angle-related coordinate values into the model as it processes A rectangle has four, changing its next-token prediction from sides to degrees. In the second, one fixed coordinate set detects hazardous requests and another steers the next token toward refusal. These examples show that MoWE combines sparse conditional computation with coordinates that can be identified and reused directly.

items.title: Functional-Group Knowledge Is Structured in Language Models Before It Is Spoken [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2611.03684v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language models serve as the reasoning core of agents for chemistry and materials science, where they must interpret molecular structure before planning syntheses or proposing materials. Yet their outputs show only what they say, not what they know. Given a prompt such as ``The primary functional group in 1-Fluorobutane (CCCCF) is'', a small general-purpose model may answer ``the alkyne group'' instead of an alkyl fluoride. The output alone cannot tell whether the model failed to recognize the fluorine or recognized it and failed to say so. We address this by reading the internal representations of five open-source models on prompts covering 92 molecules and 20 functional groups. Even without chemistry training, the models organize functional groups by chemical family, and they encode chemical differences as consistent directions. The shift from thioether ($\mathrm{R{-}S{-}R'}$) to thiol ($\mathrm{R{-}SH}$), added to ether ($\mathrm{R{-}O{-}R'}$), lands nearest alcohol ($\mathrm{R{-}OH}$). This structure emerges abruptly in the middle layers, where representations shift from tracking the wording of the prompt to tracking the functional group. The base model names the correct functional group in only 58.5\% of prompts, the lowest of the five, yet it encodes functional-group families and preserves chemically meaningful patterns. Its errors are mostly failures to answer rather than wrong answers. Functional-group knowledge is structured in the model before it is spoken. Chemistry fine-tuning reorganizes it, making functional groups rather than prompt wording dominate the representation. These results suggest that evaluating chemical language models through outputs alone can underestimate the chemical information they encode. Representation analysis can distinguish a lack of knowledge from a failure to express it, which matters when choosing or adapting models for chemical agents.

items.title: EpiLoRA: Fusing Many LoRA Adapters into Low-Precision GEMMs for Serving and RL [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2611.03899v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Low-rank adapters (LoRA) let one base model serve many fine-tuned variants: multi-tenant engines keep a single copy of the base and batch the requests of many tenants, each with its own adapter. As base models move to 8-bit (FP8) and 4-bit formats, their general matrix multiplications (GEMMs) become cheaper, but the adapters do not: engines run them as separate small GPU kernels beside the GEMM, whose latency takes a growing share of every decoding step. An adapter projects its input down to a low rank and back up, and our key observation is that the GEMM needs the down-projection only in its epilogue, the final stage in which it writes its output. EpiLoRA, a plugin for the vLLM engine, therefore launches the down-projection first and the low-precision GEMM as a dependent kernel that streams its weights meanwhile and adds every tenant's up-projection in its epilogue. On NVIDIA Hopper GPUs, EpiLoRA decodes for a single adapter with up to 24% lower time per token than vLLM's fastest configuration, and faster than SGLang and TensorRT-LLM; with many tenants, its adapter kernels deliver more throughput than vLLM's on most GPU-model pairs we tested. The same low-precision base also trains: a LoRA reinforcement-learning trainer that computes on the engine's FP8 weights needs no 16-bit copy, so a 27B model trains on one 48 GB GPU, and an engine that then keeps activations in 16 bits removes most of the remaining mismatch between the model generating training data and the one trained.

items.title: Must AI Spell It Out? Pragmatic Comprehension of Alerts in a Time-Critical Task [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2611.03976v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Assistive systems typically tell users everything, often spending time and attention on what a user already knows, leaving less for what happens next. People, on the other hand, leave out what they expect the listener can supply. Can people use their prior knowledge to understand an incomplete message when the speaker is a machine though? We studied this pragmatic comprehension in a monitoring task controlling users' prior knowledge and the available time to detect critical situations. In a preregistered study (N=114), we compared a pragmatic planner that reasons over a model of the listener's knowledge to decide what to say, when, and how explicitly, with a baseline specifying problems fully in onset order. Participants resolved underspecified alerts almost as reliably as fully specified ones and sooner, detected more problems, and rated the pragmatic assistant helpful more often, with no increase in reported mental demand. Our findings show that people can recover what the system left implicit and that pragmatic communication can support effective assistance under the constraints of a changing world.

items.title: When Strong Reasoners Join the Pool: Small Union Premiums and Costly Runaway Generations in LLM Routing [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2611.04098v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Routing benchmarks often judge a router against a hindsight oracle that counts a query as solved whenever any model's recorded answer is correct, but under stochastic decoding that oracle mixes two different objects: the clairvoyant ceiling of committing to one model per query and the premium of calling several models and keeping any correct answer. A companion study measured this premium at 3.5 percentage points (pp) for 11 small open models on MATH-500; how large it is once current reasoning models enter the pool was unknown. We measure it with a fixed-protocol, pre-committed generation on a single NVIDIA B300: all 500 MATH-500 problems, 30 seeded samples per problem, Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct and NVIDIA's Nemotron Nano 9B v2 and Nemotron Super 49B v1.5 (a NAS derivative of the same 70B) under vendor sampling, a 65,536-token cap, a pinned Math-Verify scorer, and an append-only attempt ledger, for 45,000 scored responses. The two reasoning models both reach 96.1% accuracy against 76.2% for the 70B baseline. The empirical product-coupling premium is 0.215-0.588 pp across all two- and three-model pools; the empirical plug-in selection headroom over always calling Nano is 1.27 pp; and resampling Nano three times gives practically the same empirical any-correct rate as calling all three models once. Only 31 responses reached the cap, 25 of them with exactly periodic tails, yet the capped responses account for up to 60.2% of a model's output-length-squared proxy, and long generations made a fourth planned model, Llama-3.1-8B, too slow to finish. The premium is far below the companion's 3.5 pp, but models, pool size and protocol changed together; an oracle gap should therefore be reported with the pool, the protocol, the samples per cell and the decoding budget that produced it.

items.title: LoopKV: Loop-Aware KV Cache Compression for Serving Looped Transformers [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2611.04137v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Looped transformers apply a shared block several times per token to improve accuracy without adding parameters. For models such as Ouro that keep a separate key-value (KV) cache per loop, cache memory limits the batch size that amortizes repeated weight reads. Uniform-bit quantization and fixed rules per loop do not allocate precision according to each layer's sensitivity in each loop. Measurements on Ouro show that quantization sensitivity varies across (loop, layer) cells, and the sum of individual cell damages approximates the overall output damage. Sharing damage also varies by cell, with later loops generally tolerating sharing better. Skipping low-attention values to save reads produces errors that compound across loops. LoopKV uses a one-time offline profile to choose 4-bit storage, 2-bit storage or reuse of the final loop's KV for each cell. The planner minimizes reads under budgets for predicted damage and storage. During decoding, each loop reads the high 2 bits of each 4-bit value and fetches the low bits only where its own attention weights require 4-bit precision. A single fused kernel in vLLM executes the plan. Serving Ouro-1.4B on one RTX PRO 6000, the memory-optimized LoopKV-M plan stores 35% less KV than uniform 4-bit quantization (KIVI-4) on the same fused kernel and CUDA graph. It sustains 1.7-2.2x KIVI-4's goodput under a latency service-level objective with a 16K-token maximum length. None of its averages on six public benchmarks falls significantly below BF16's.

items.title: Neologism Inoculation Prompting [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2611.04260v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Inoculation prompting is a method to reduce undesired behaviours such as reward hacking in frontier models. It works by training a model on harmful examples under a prompt that specifies the undesired behaviour, which reduces the model's tendency to exhibit it unless prompted. However, the inoculation prompt is written in plain English, so any user can re-elicit the behaviour easily. We introduce neologism inoculation prompting (NIP), which replaces the English prompt with a new token that is trained on the frozen model and removed at deployment. NIP outperforms other inoculation methods, and performs competitively with gradient routing despite being simpler. It also works on reward hacking, but fails on sycophancy and harassment. Using control tokens and analyses of activations, we identify the mechanism for this as NIP hiding the harmful behaviour behind an unreachable region of model inputs, rather than deleting it. More broadly, our work suggests that neologisms can be a powerful way to carve out and shape access to behaviours that are undesired or harmful.

items.title: Sketchpad: certified exact arithmetic with a small vision-language model [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2611.04434v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language models are accurate on most long-arithmetic problems, but their accuracy is estimated on samples and carries no guarantee for an unseen input; tool use is exact but moves the computation outside the network. We show that exactness at all input lengths becomes a finite, checkable property of a network when each of its steps reads only a bounded view of an external working memory. In Sketchpad, Qwen3.5-0.8B with a low-rank adapter executes arithmetic procedures on a rendered sheet. Each forward pass reads a three-cell view and emits one step: a digit, a carry or borrow, and the next operation. A fixed runtime moves the view and writes no digit of a result. We prove in Lean that the model is then exact on all inputs of any length if and only if it is exact on the finite set of views the runtime presents, that no finite test suffices when steps also read earlier steps, and that the guarantee tolerates bounded numerical perturbation and extends to compositions of procedures. All 2,446 views pass on the deployment device, a laptop GPU running the model in a web browser. The certified model performs signed addition and subtraction, long multiplication and division, square roots and greatest common divisors at arbitrary length. It solved 200 of 200 pre-registered problems in the browser, and 220 of 220 sums of up to 1,000 digits and products of up to 20 digits, of which GPT-6.1 Sol, the strongest of ten other models, solved 217. A symbolic runtime built on these procedures solves, expands and factors polynomials with every number computed by the model, and a multiplicative gate on the adapter recovers the base model exactly when the sheet is not in use.

items.title: Near-Zero Token Embeddings Silently Stall Training in Gated Sequence Models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2611.04449v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Among 291 surveyed open-weight language model repositories (280 distinct embedding tables), 52.6% of untied gated and hybrid checkpoints (20/38) contain reachable input embeddings with norms below $10^{-6}$, compared with 0% of weight-tied models. Such near-zero rows can arise during pretraining when unseen rare or template tokens receive zero input gradients while AdamW weight decay shrinks untied embeddings. In tested Transformer configurations, non-initial positions or a BOS token prevent this failure mode. In gated sequence models (Mamba, Gated DeltaNet, xLSTM), a near-zero token can amplify input-embedding gradients by more than 30 orders of magnitude (up to 35). At zero input, current-token readout factors (SiLU gates or linear queries) vanish, suppressing historical-state readout. Residual RMS values can then fall below the square root of the RMSNorm floor across consecutive layers, causing Pre-RMSNorm to amplify backward gradients by up to $10^3$ per layer. When a gradient entry exceeds $1.84 \times 10^{19}$, FP32 global-norm clipping in PyTorch, Hugging Face Trainer, and FSDP2 can overflow to infinity and zero the current batch's gradients. In Telugu continual pretraining of Nemotron-3-Nano-4B, this discards updates on approximately 20% of steps and leaves triggered rows frozen. We propose two remedies. For released checkpoints, GroupClip decouples input-embedding clipping using a 64-bit or rescaled norm; its rescaled implementation eliminates update loss and heals triggered rows in one step with negligible measured end-to-end overhead. For pretraining, GateFloor ($\mathrm{SiLU}(z) + \delta$, $\delta \in [0.01, 0.1]$) keeps the gate positive at zero input, reducing near-zero gradients by 28 orders of magnitude in experiments up to 370M parameters, with perplexity comparable to the baseline.

items.title: Large Language Model-Assisted Adaptive Heuristic Search for Agile Earth Observation Satellite Scheduling [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2611.04458v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agile Earth observation satellites must coordinate imaging tasks within limited observation windows, while accounting for attitude maneuvering and onboard energy constraints. Competition among observation opportunities makes scheduling performance sensitive to the heuristic rules used for task selection. This letter proposes a large language model (LLM)-assisted adaptive heuristic search method for agile Earth observation satellite scheduling. The LLM generates an initial heuristic rule according to the characteristics of the scheduling instance. During the subsequent ant colony search, search performance and scheduling information are fed back to the LLM to refine the heuristic rule. The proposed modifications are evaluated through paired solution constructions before being incorporated into the search process. A unified scheduling procedure determines task selection, satellite assignment, and observation timing under the operational constraints. Experiments on six scheduling scenarios involving 50--200 imaging tasks demonstrate that the proposed method achieves 4.3\%--9.6\% higher mean observation benefit than the strongest baseline.

items.title: $\tau$-Rec-Books: A Disclosure-Controlled Benchmark for Requirement Elicitation in Agentic Recommender Systems [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2611.04459v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: While conversational recommendation systems provide a more natural user interface, they face the challenge of progressively discovering a user's needs before they can recommend an item that satisfies them. To evaluate the ability of AI agents at this elicitation process, we introduce $\tau$-Rec-Books, a benchmark that holds each user request fixed while varying only when the user reveals their requirements: all at the start (volunteer), one at the start and the rest when asked (mixed), or some never (hidden). A hidden requirement can be found only by proposing books and inferring it from the user's accept or reject verdicts. We generate 450 tasks over a catalog of 20,000 books from Wikidata, develop a rule-based simulated user to answer the agent, and score recommendations against catalog metadata without an LLM judge. Across four agents and two search interfaces, success rates fall for every agent and interface, on average from 0.975 (volunteer) to 0.756 (mixed) and 0.283 (hidden). Mixed tasks fail mainly because agents do not ask, and when told to ask, every agent reaches at least 0.931. On hidden tasks, most failures come from agents recommending a book they never proposed to the user. When told to propose first, agents only match a simple baseline that proposes popular books, and stay well below one that uses rejection to rule out possible requirements. We release the catalog pipeline, task generator, simulated user, validators, reference agents, and all agent traces at https://github.com/nbharaths/tau-rec/tree/main/data/tracks/books-wikidata-v2.

items.title: Self-Privileged Fine-Tuning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2611.04632v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is a key component of language model post-training, enabling effective task adaptation and serving as an important foundation for subsequent reinforcement learning. Recent methods seek to improve SFT by introducing token-level weights into the training objective, where these weights are typically derived from a model's output distribution at each token position. To better understand how such weighting schemes affect SFT, we analyze their optimization objectives and theoretically characterize the target distributions they induce. Our analysis shows that dynamic weighting methods, such as Dynamic Fine-Tuning (DFT), induce a heavily sharpened distribution, whereas static weighting methods fit a target distribution proportional to the product of the data distribution and a frozen prior. These findings suggest that static weighting provides a more stable training target, while its effectiveness critically depends on the quality of the prior distribution. Building on this observation, we propose Self-Privileged Fine-Tuning (SPFT), which uses a frozen copy of the initial model conditioned on privileged information (such as ground truth for mathematical questions) as a prior to provide guidance for token-level weighting during fine-tuning. Through a Bayesian decomposition, we further show that SPFT reweights the standard static prior according to how informative each target token is for predicting the ground-truth outcome, thereby assigning larger weights to more predictive tokens. Experiments on mathematical reasoning and code generation show that SPFT improves over standard SFT and other baselines across the main settings.

items.title: Where Is the Truth When AI Agents Disagree? Dependence-Aware Belief Propagation for Unsupervised Truth Discovery (Extended Version) [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2611.04805v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM agents often give conflicting answers to the same question, and many deployed agents are variants of one base model, so their errors are correlated. We study truth discovery among such agents: inferring the true answer and each agent's reliability without labels. Classical truth-discovery and crowdsourcing estimators reward an agreeing bloc and can fall below majority vote. We propose BP-TD, which adds per-agent decorrelation weights to mean-field variational inference on a one-coin Dawid-Skene model, so that agents sharing a base model count together as about one vote. Its first iteration is exactly a weighted vote; later iterations estimate agent reliability. With 13 local agents on MMLU, BP-TD beats majority vote without any labels (0.716 vs. 0.624 on 160 questions; 0.707 vs. 0.674 on 10,000) and ranks agents by their true accuracy, which classical estimators invert. The gain depends on the pool: over 2,852 sub-pools of four benchmarks, decorrelation helps when the largest correlated bloc is weaker than the other agents and hurts when it is the strongest, and we found no label-free statistic that tells the two cases apart. Labels change the picture quickly: with 20 labelled questions, selecting the single best agent is more accurate than every aggregator we tested on MMLU, ARC and TruthfulQA.

items.title: Think Less, Locally: Local Preference Learning for Reasoning Compression [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2611.04814v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large reasoning models achieve strong performance on challenging tasks, but their long chain-of-thought often incurs substantial inference costs by continuing to deliberate after sufficient information has been obtained.
